extraction.research_question: RQ1: What are the key characteristics and trends of research in the academic debate on lobbying coalitions? RQ2: What are the main explanations used to account for interest groups' choice to form or join a coalition? (p. 3)
extraction.theory: No single theory is adopted. The authors say the field is implicitly shaped by a rationalist framework with methodological individualism (fn. 13, p. 9). Hypotheses are sorted into macro, meso and micro levels, plus composite hypotheses. The 'weapon of the weak' argument (weaker groups pool resources; Hanegraaff and Pritoni 2019) is the central tested proposition. Interest-group definitions follow Truman (1951) and Berry (1977); coalition definitions follow Junk (2020b): policy camp, behavioral coordination, or formal organization.
extraction.data: Web of Science Core Collection, English-language 'article' documents, 1 Jan 1985 to 31 Dec 2023, title/keyword search for lobby, coalition, interest, group, alliance, restricted to Political Science and Public Administration categories. Initial hits N=45; after abstract screening N=34 eligible; after snowballing N=80 final sample (unit: article). Coded by two researchers with a codebook. Meta-analysis subsample: 16 articles, 77 theoretical hypotheses (unit: hypothesis), restricted to articles that treat coalition formation as the dependent variable, use behavioral or organizational definitions, use the individual group or lobbyist as unit, and test hypotheses empirically.
extraction.method: PRISMA-ScR scoping review protocol (Tricco et al. 2018) with descriptive counts (year, venue, polity, design, definitions) and a vote-count style meta-analysis: for each hypothesis, supported or not supported; confirmation rate = supported / total by level, factor and decade. Intercoder reliability by Krippendorff's alpha on 8 randomly selected articles (10% of sample): K-alpha = 0.889 (p. 4). Decade assignment uses article publication year.
extraction.identification: Not applicable: descriptive literature review with no causal identification strategy. The authors frame coalition formation as the dependent variable and note that the influence-of-coalitions question is left for future work (pp. 9, 15).
extraction.scope: Population: English-language articles in WoS political science and public administration journals on interest groups and lobbying coalitions, 1985-2023 (excludes sociology, economics and business journals, books, chapters and grey literature; fn. 3, 4, 17). Geography dominated by the US (41 of 80) and EU (25 of 80). Era: 1985-2023, decades 1990s, 2000s, 2010s, 2020s.

limitations: WoS Core Collection starts in 1985; pre-1985 literature is excluded (p. 14).
Restriction to political science and public administration journals may exclude relevant work in other fields; sociology journals on nonprofits are excluded on purpose (fn. 4, fn. 17).
Books, book chapters and grey literature are excluded, which the authors say may bias the sample toward quantitative studies (fn. 3).
Snowball sampling introduces path dependence toward older, more-cited articles (fn. 5, fn. 7); more than half of the final sample came from snowballing (p. 5).
Keyword expansion (advocacy, organisation, pressure) added only 6 articles, which the authors read as validating the search terms (fn. 2).
Publication bias toward US and EU studies is acknowledged (fn. 10).
Hypothesis meta-analysis uses a dichotomy (supported or not), losing granularity about strength and limits (p. 14).
Only 16 of 80 articles enter the hypothesis analysis, and hypotheses are counted rather than weighted by study quality.
Intercoder reliability was checked on only 8 articles (10%) (p. 4).
Field fragmentation: the authors note many hypotheses and a lack of one unified framework, which may explain the mixed findings (fn. 13).

summary_md:
Pritoni, Bitonti and Montalbano run a PRISMA-ScR scoping review of 80 English-language political science and public administration articles on lobbying coalitions, published 1985-2023 and indexed in Web of Science. Sixteen of those articles, contributing 77 hypotheses, enter a vote-count meta-analysis. Large-N quantitative designs dominate the field: 42 of 80 articles (52.5%). Social network analysis appears in only 4 of 80 (5%), and QCA in none. Most studies define coalitions by behavior: 59 of 80 use behavioral coordination, 12 use policy camp and 6 use formal organization. Across all 77 hypotheses, 57 are supported (74%). That figure pools US and EU studies and is UNSTRATIFIED by polity. By level, support is meso 11/14, micro 35/45 and macro 10/16. The 'weapon of the weak' hypothesis is supported in 11 of 12 tests, though a minority of studies find the reverse, and the authors suggest a minimum-resource threshold. Issue context is supported 6/7, ideology 6/7 and third-party brokers 3/3. The SNA-based tests have the weakest record of any design, 5 of 9 supported (55.6%). The review studies only why groups form coalitions. It calls the evidence on whether coalitions win contradictory and leaves that question to future work.

For Paul's systems, the paper matters because the coalitions it studies are coalitions among interest groups. Melange's 'coalitions' are mostly blocs of legislators: Ward clusters on press lean, signed partitions, and cosponsor spread. Read strictly, the review supports two narrower points about how Melange models the industries themselves. First, coalition alignment depends on the issue, which favors the per-bill contested registry over fixed global sides. Second, the CU side is modeled as a lone actor, even though the literature says weaker groups pool resources. The review gives no evidence that coalitions raise influence, so neither point justifies adding allied money as a weight.

bearings.paper_claim: Junk's (2020b) typology separates three coalition definitions: policy camp (shared positions only; 12/80 articles), behavioral coordination (59/80) and formal organization (6/80). In the reviewed literature the unit that forms a coalition is the interest group or the lobbyist, not the legislator.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 7-9; definitional counts p. 9 and p. 13
bearings.system_side: detect_coalitions runs Ward.D2 on legislators' recency-weighted graded press scores, with aggregate lean weighted x3, and labels the resulting blocs 'coalitions'. Nothing in it observes coordination. In Junk's terms it is at most a legislator 'policy camp'. The file now labels blocs pro-credit-union, hostile-to-credit-union or mixed. The brain note says all blocs are labelled pro-CU, which looks stale relative to this file.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper gives a definition only and does not validate the policy-camp reading. Its findings concern groups choosing allies, so its determinants (weakness, brokers) should not be read onto legislator blocs. If the blocs keep the name 'coalition', the label should say they are shared-position clusters with no coordination evidence.

gaps_exposed: Melange has no model of coalition formation among interest groups. Credit unions are a single actor, and the other industries are fixed 'opposition' in every context (build_opposition_prior.py:68-75). The literature's main determinants (relative weakness, issue salience and conflict, ideological propensity, third-party brokers) are not represented.
The contested-bills schema cannot record an allied industry on a bill, only counterparties (contested_bills.py:175-176). Strange-bedfellow alignments therefore cannot be stored.

The system has no group-to-group broker layer. Third-party brokers are the factor with the most uniform support (3/3), but no Melange component represents brokerage between interest groups. The staffer-network 'bridging' measure concerns staff layers and must not be read as brokerage or introduction access (D-025).

Several components call legislator clusters 'coalitions' (Ward blocs, signed partitions, cosponsor coalition spread). The review's definitional typology shows that none of them records coordination, so the term should be scoped wherever it is displayed.
flags: D-021: the natural way to operationalize 'behavioral coordination' coalitions from Melange data would be an industry-to-industry graph from co-registration on the same bills or issue codes in LDA. That would use LDA as an edge or weight source, which D-021 bars. LDA may only identify allies, never connect or weight them.

The paper's call for more SNA (Paul highlighted 'SNA and QCA') is not evidence that SNA works. SNA-based hypotheses have the lowest confirmation rate in Table 5: 5 of 9 (55.6%), versus 74% overall. Quote that only with its denominator. The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization), so nothing needs flagging on that front.
The 74% overall confirmation rate and the 91.7% weapon-of-the-weak rate pool US (41/80) and EU (25/80) studies. They are vote counts unweighted by study quality and should be quoted as UNSTRATIFIED.

Staleness: the component card and brain note say all Ward blocs are labelled pro-CU (a known mislabel). The current R file at cu_press_release_scraper.R:3193-3195 labels blocs as pro, hostile or mixed by mean bloc lean. Which version produced the live output is UNVERIFIED and needs a second check (DE-062).

Any pairing of this review with Melange (for example, CUs as the 'weaker' group by the joined LDA totals of ABA $228M vs CUNA $93M, vintage 2024-10-25 with coverage reliable through 2021) is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul recorded no takeaways for this paper; both annotation entries are citation-only. His highlights stress three points: SNA is underused, coalitions form around salient, conflictual issues, and third-party brokers matter. The component map attaches the paper to melange-sna.press-coalition-ward. That link merges two different coalition concepts. Pritoni reviews coalitions among interest groups, while the Ward component clusters legislators by press lean, which is at most a 'policy camp' with no coordination evidence. The paper's real implications lie elsewhere. It supports the per-bill contested registry (issue-specific alignment) and exposes a gap: the CU side is modeled as a lone actor with all other industries fixed as opposition. Paul's highlight on SNA underuse should not be taken as an endorsement of SNA. In this review SNA studies have the lowest hypothesis support rate (5/9). His note does not reflect the current bloc labels in the R code (pro, hostile and mixed now exist), and the brain card's 'all blocs pro-CU' description may also be stale.

related.why: Aref and Neal detect coalitions among House members through signed partitions, which is the legislator-level sense of 'coalition'. Pritoni covers the interest-group sense. Together they show that Melange's 'coalition' components use the legislator concept.
This is the earlier signed-partition method behind melange-sna.signed-coalitions. It works at the legislator level, so Pritoni's determinants do not transfer to it.

Kim et al.'s per-bill Support/Oppose/Engage positions from LDA reports would be the way to observe Pritoni's issue-specific group alignments, such as who stands with CUs on a given bill. D-021 still limits LDA to identity, not edges.
Romero Moreno is the stated basis for the contested-bills counterparty term. Pritoni supplies the empirical case that counterparties should be set per issue rather than globally.
Azaiez applies network (hypergraph) methods to EU lobby co-participation, which is the kind of SNA-on-group-coalitions work Pritoni says is rare (4 of 80 articles).
This is a statistical network analysis of lobbying communities, one answer to Pritoni's call for SNA of lobbying coalitions in US data.
It is cited alongside Pritoni for the same component (press-coalition-ward). It infers communities from shared text, which is again a policy-camp-style definition rather than coordination.

extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. Firm-size and stage results are conditional associations. The paper frames them as associations that call for further study. Stage timing relies on an assumption: lobbying in a quarterly report is directed at the bill's most recent legislative stage, with the report deadline used as the timing proxy (p.5).
extraction.coverage: Full text read: every line of the extracted text (about 3,280 numbered lines), covering main text pp.1-9, references 1-34, and SI Appendices 1-6 (Tables 2-21, Figs 7-12). Both annotation files were read in full: E = ef8b6c693fc3.json (99 highlights) and A = a60235faab0f.json (112 highlights plus 1 free-text note). Both are authored by Paul Goff and overlap heavily, so paul_markup groups items by passage; every E and A index is accounted for. Highlight colour meaning is not recorded in the files (Y = yellow, G = green, P = pink, B = blue). Covered text is paraphrased, not quoted, to respect the copyright limit. Extraction artifacts (stray tokens such as FT, DRA, RAF, and split words) are treated as text-layer noise.
extraction.research_question: Can the positions that U.S. interest groups take on individual bills (Support, Oppose, or Engage, where Engage = Amend + Monitor) be measured directly from Lobbying Disclosure Act reports across all bills from the 111th to 117th Congresses? The paper then asks how those positions vary by legislative stage, firm size, bill subject, and industry.
extraction.theory: No formal model is stated. Framing draws on cited work: lobbying as a legislative subsidy (ref 3); firm size shapes corporate political activity through fixed and variable costs, affecting both whether firms lobby and which positions they take (refs 30, 31); lobbying varies by legislative stage (refs 27, 28; ex post lobbying, ref 29); legislative and lobbying networks predict political activity (refs 14, 21); latent preferences are estimated from positions the way roll-call ideal points are (refs 22, 23); donation-based ideology measures may not reflect expressed policy stances (refs 17, 18).
extraction.data: Sample: LDA quarterly lobbying reports filed 2009-2022 (111th-117th Congresses), collected from the Senate Office of Public Records and linked to bill metadata from Congress.gov. About 1.4 million bill-line text pairs before a keyword filter. Final dataset: 279,104 bill positions; 12,032 interest groups; 42,475 bills. Unit: interest group x bill pair. LLM-labelled set: 82,421 positions (6,495 groups; 22,820 bills). GNN-labelled set: 196,683 positions (11,185 groups; 36,824 bills), about 70.5% of all positions. Validation: 391 samples on which two human coders agreed; 1,182 interest group-bill pairs overlap MapLight. GNN training: 22,635 MapLight pairs (18,180 Support, 4,455 Oppose). LPscore sample: 1,796 groups and 2,020 bills. Firm analysis: Compustat firm-year data, 2009-2022, 5,421-7,014 firms per year. CFscore comparison: 218 identically named groups. Bill final-status counts (Table 13, SI p.14): Enacted 715 bills (3,640 groups); Vetoed 3 bills (162 groups); Passed 28 bills (128 groups); Provisionally Killed 74 bills (473 groups).
extraction.method: (1) LLM labelling: GPT-4 via Azure OpenAI at temperature 0, zero-shot prompt with bill ID, short and official titles, and lobbying text. Five labels in the LLM stage (Support, Oppose, Amend, Monitor, Mention); Mention covers ambiguous or non-amending activity. (2) GNN refinement: heterogeneous GraphSAGE (SI Table 9: 3 classes, hidden size 90, ELU, dropout 0.2, concat decoder) predicts the interest group-bill link type (Support, Oppose, Engage). Amend and Monitor are merged into Engage because four-class accuracy on Amend was low. Training uses LLM labels plus MapLight labels, with a 7:1:2 split. Seventeen graph configurations are compared (base graph; add sponsors, legislators, registrants, lobbyists, related bills, and combinations); the best is base graph + legislator-lobbyist. Predictions are kept as proxy labels only when class probability exceeds 0.9. (3) LPscores: graded-response IRT (Samejima; R mirt) on Support and Oppose labels, with Engage excluded, after keeping groups with at least 10 bills and bills with at least 10 groups. (4) Analyses: descriptive position shares by legislative stage (Fig 2; stage timing proxied by quarterly report deadline); logistic regression for the decision to lobby and Dirichlet regression for position composition, with predicted-probability differences between firms at the 90th and 10th employment percentiles (Fig 3; year FE; optional NAICS FE, PPENT, COGS; SI Tables 19-20); descriptive position ratios by subject (Fig 4, SI Table 21); LPscore distributions by industry (Fig 5); bill-level latent-score scatter and KDE (Fig 6); Pearson correlation with DIME CFscores (n=218).
extraction.scope: Population: U.S. federal interest groups that filed LDA reports on named bills (S. and H.R. bills), 2009-2022 (111th-117th Congresses). Firm analysis: Compustat-listed companies only. Institutions: Congress (committee, floor, enactment, veto stages) and the executive via presidential action. Groups that do not file lobbying reports are outside the dataset, which the paper highlights when comparing with MapLight.

summary_md:
Kim, Kim, Jeong, Oh and In Song Kim (arXiv 2025, PNAS-format draft) label which way interest groups lean on individual bills, using the free-text bill lines in LDA quarterly reports from 2009 to 2022 (111th-117th Congresses). The pipeline has two stages. GPT-4 at temperature 0 labels keyword-filtered lines, producing 82,421 positions. A heterogeneous GraphSAGE model then fills in where the text is unclear, producing 196,683 more, about 70.5% of the total. The final dataset has 279,104 group-by-bill positions covering 12,032 groups and 42,475 bills, labelled Support, Oppose, or Engage (Engage merges Amend and Monitor). The LLM agrees with human coders 96.9% of the time, but only on the 391 items where both coders agreed. It matches MapLight on 91% of 1,182 overlapping pairs. The GNN reaches 78.5% accuracy, and Oppose is its weakest class (F1 64). On the substance:
- Support rises toward enactment.
- Oppose and Amend rise late in bills that go on to fail. That finding rests on 3 vetoed bills.
- Comparing firms at the 90th and 10th percentiles of size, larger firms are 19.5 pp more likely to lobby and 4.5 pp more likely to Monitor.
- A one-dimensional IRT score for groups (LPscore) correlates only weakly with DIME CFscores (r = 0.19, n = 218).

This matters here because the system has already taken in this dataset and copied its method. It downloaded the Dataverse release, rebuilt Kim's labelling step with Haiku, and benchmarked it against Kim's published labels at natural base rates. On that benchmark, Support and Oppose come out weak (precision 0.42, recall 0.49) and Amend is never recovered. That result led to the standing rule that inferred positions are evidence for retrieval and adjudication, never automatic weights. The paper's real value to Paul is as calibration gold for 2009-2022 and as raw material for per-bill industry conflict, which the system already computes. It is not a feed that can be wired straight into the graph.

Source: "Machine Learning & Sentiment Analysis - Annotated Bibliography" (sha12 b0774147a262), read in full from C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\annotations\. The sidecar C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\b0774147a262.json does not exist, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights to fold in. The document lists 8 cited works. Only 4 (Birkenmaier and Lechner; Kim et al.; Peng et al.; Ramey et al.) have annotation text. The other 4 (Alkazzi and Okumura; Joo and Steinert-Threlkeld; Taherdoost and Madanchian; Steinert-Threlkeld) are citation-only.

Overarching argument: Paul treats machine learning and NLP applied to public political text (congressional floor speech, public statements, lobbying filings) as a way to produce actor-level attributes (personality traits, policy positions, emotion) that can be placed on nodes of a social-network-analysis graph. The purpose he names is political intelligence: lobbying strategy, industry alignment, and how to pitch policy to a specific member of Congress.

Research questions and gaps Paul states:
1. Conversion step. Birkenmaier and Lechner, Peng et al., and Ramey et al. each say the pipeline does not specify how a model's output becomes a graph node or vector. This is the most repeated gap in the document.
2. Ambiguity. Birkenmaier and Lechner say the method does not separate ambiguous statements.
3. Conflict. Kim et al. do not show inter-industry conflict over a specific bill, which Paul says matters for political intelligence.
4. Temporal lag. Kim et al. are reactive, not predictive, because filing reports lag current positions.
5. Model limits. Peng et al. say long-distance dependency is the main obstacle for most emotion models; stacking reduces but does not remove it.
6. Venue coverage. Ramey et al. offer no pipeline for textual venues beyond their own, and Paul says a framework for contextual or auditory constraints is also needed.

Synthesis: Birkenmaier and Lechner and Ramey et al. both concern personality measurement from speech or text, with Ramey et al. as the older foundation and Birkenmaier and Lechner as the newer, codebook-backed method. Kim et al. and Birkenmaier and Lechner both concern the actor-to-graph link. Peng et al. supplies the model landscape that the other two would run on.

Self-declared gap: Paul says his own technical grounding is not yet sufficient for Peng et al. and plans a second reading after more background.

Path-finding link: Alkazzi and Okumura is the only multi-agent path-finding item. Paul wrote no annotation for it, so any link to Melange path-finding is not in his words.

Overarching argument: Paul's reading treats the literature as a stack that feeds his systems in order: (1) measuring traits or positions from text, (2) turning text and filings into network nodes and edges, (3) finding paths and communities in that graph, (4) using influence and lobbying-return evidence to set allocation and fundraising targets. Research questions Paul raises: how to convert an individual's text-derived trait score into a social-network node (Birkenmaier); how to disentangle ambiguous statements; how to turn a bipartite lobbying model into a graph that path-finding can run on (Kim and Kunisky); how to treat negative sentiment in influence edges and how to score agreement between actors when sentiment is negative (Fink); whether reply and mention edges are negative; how to add temporal weighting so shifting relationships are captured (Fink, Malaterre); how to separate campaign donations from events and meetings in return models (Huneeus and Kim); whether the allocation model should differentiate representatives by state-layer industry presence (Huneeus and Kim); whether ideologically aligned think-tank funding should enter allocation models (Furnas et al.).

Syntheses across works: Louvain community detection recurs in Ardekani et al. and Malaterre and Lareau, and Paul applies it to communities and coalitions. Two works share the author In Song Kim (Huneeus and Kim; Kim and Kunisky), and Paul's notes on them connect lobbying returns to network structure. Kim et al. The file does not name Moneyball, Mentat, Terrier, or path-finding; the only system-facing language is "social network analysis vector graph" and "future allocation models". Taken together, the commentary argues four things. Lobbying pays: firms that lobby for beneficial legislation see large returns (Alexander), lobbying lifts revenue and concentration (Huneeus and Kim; Bickmore), with the revenue gain partly at the expense of the wider economy. Access and influence are bought through donations, and the effect is strongest for committee-related activity and fades unless renewed (Kim, In Song et al.). Information is filtered by staffers' ideology, so advocacy should be routed through ideologically aligned think tanks; Paul proposes treating think-tank funding like venture capital in allocation models. Existing position-mapping pipelines (Kim, Jiseon et al.) are useful for SNA but reactive and blind to inter-industry conflict over a bill, which Paul calls vital for political intelligence. The implied research questions are: does lobbying pay, and for whom (size, industry); do donations buy legislative involvement, and how durable is it; does the information source matter; and can position data be used predictively. Stated gaps: no predictive capability, no conflict detection, and no link yet from these findings to specific Melange, Moneyball, or Mentat components.

bearings.paper_claim: LLM labels agree with human coders at 96.93% accuracy and F1 97.19, but only on the 391 samples where two coders agreed. MapLight concordance is 91.03% on 1,182 pairs and only covers Support/Oppose, and those pairs also trained the GNN. GNN per-class F1: Support 79.19, Oppose 64.06, Engage 80.70.
bearings.paper_location: Validation p.3; Link Type Prediction p.4; SI Tables 11-12
bearings.system_side: Gold-set validation is meant to measure accuracy at natural base rates and on adversarial frames (for example, the 0.571 goldeval figure for DEBATE). The system's own benchmark of the Kim-format Haiku lane uses the 876 pairs that overlap Kim's published end results. It splits Kim's llm and gnn annotation lanes and does no stratification. It reports three-class accuracy carried by the majority Engage class, Support/Oppose precision 0.42 and recall 0.49, and Amend 0 found of 23.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's validation design picks out clear-cut texts, so its headline accuracy does not carry over to Mention, Amend, or ambiguous lines. The system's benchmark compares Haiku with Kim's labels, not with human truth, and 541 of the 876 pairs are GNN-labelled, so the reference set is itself about 78% accurate. Read the system's numbers as agreement with Kim, not as accuracy. Both are UNVERIFIED as accuracy until a human-gold path reproduces them (DE-062).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-validation#Gold-set validation and zero-rank-delta gate|Gold-set validation and zero-rank-delta gate]]

bearings.paper_claim: Oppose is the hardest class (GNN F1 in the 60s across all 17 graph configurations), because it is rare. Engage dominates the GNN-labelled set: 137,023 of 188,639 Engage labels (72.6%) come from the GNN. Industries with conflicting interests sit at opposite ends of the LPscore axis (Fig 5).
bearings.paper_location: SI Appendix 2 pp.12-14; Table 1 p.3; Analysis 4 p.7 Fig 5
bearings.system_side: Tensor cells on the industry boards are signed by adjudication. Positions in Kim's format are joined only with the basis tag inferred_<variant>. The standing rule is that they serve retrieval and adjudication only, never automatic weights. The bank-column pilot found about 70% of Oppose labels were wrong when checked against primary text, and it signed zero new rows.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds for Oppose labels on finance-sector bills from both GPT-4 and Haiku readers. The paper reports Oppose weakness for the GNN stage. The system observed it for its own LLM lane on 2021-2026 text. Both point the same way, but they are different readers on different eras.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-labels-and-tiers#Per-industry tier boards, industry-axes tensor and crown law|Per-industry tier boards, industry-axes tensor and crown law]]

bearings.paper_claim: Bill-level positions show opposing industries on the same bill. On environmental bills, environmental groups Oppose while commercial groups Support. Subject Oppose ratios: Public lands 0.354 (51 bills), Environmental protection 0.280 (108 bills). The paper does not tabulate conflict between industries on a given bill.
bearings.paper_location: Analysis 3 p.6-7 (Fig 4, SI Table 21); Analysis 4 p.7-9 (Fig 5-6)
bearings.system_side: The contested-bills registry is a loader for per-bill counterparty sets that Paul ratifies. No engine consumes it; the bundle reads it for display only. Separately, org_stance_priors recomputes ALIGNED, OPPOSED, and UNKNOWN per bill for each pair of directional sectors. It uses Kim's historical label_3_class plus current inferred signs, and it hard-fails if a CCCA anchor bill reads OPPOSED for the bank|credit_union pair.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Kim's data runs only through the 117th Congress (2022), so it can nominate candidate contested bills from the past and calibrate the alliance-conflict recompute. Current bills depend on the weaker Haiku lane. Admission to the registry stays an owner ruling. An OPPOSED pair from inferred labels is a lead, not a fact.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-lobbying#Contested-bills registry|Contested-bills registry]]

bearings.paper_claim: Positions are measured as interest group x bill. Legislators and sponsors enter only as context nodes in the GNN graph, and the best configuration adds legislator-lobbyist prior-work ties. The paper never measures a position or contact between a group and a member.
bearings.system_side: The member-year lobbying link maps a client to every sponsor and cosponsor of a lobbied bill. That makes P(joined | lobbied) = 1, so it is REFUTED as influence evidence. build_dyad_signs routes inferred org-bill signs through the same sponsor and cosponsor rosters, counting p_support >= 0.7 as support and <= 0.3 as oppose. efficiency_layers then z-scores the resulting signed_non_cu_opposition_count as one of its contest_index components.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Kim's measure stops at the bill. Pushing it onto members through the bill roster brings back the circularity the system already refuted, so the dyad counts describe what bills members sponsored, not whom an org targeted. Kim's legislator-lobbyist relation is a revolving-door edge, so influence language is barred on it.

bearings.system_side: A bill's CU direction comes from a 60-row hand table (cfpb_bill_directions.csv, Reduce +1 / Expand -1) plus the BILLS table in the R scraper. The member-prior override was rejected (0.839 to 0.770 held-out).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Useful as an external audit of the hand-set direction table, but only for bills in the 111th-117th Congresses that CUNA or NAFCU named in LD-2 lines. 118th and 119th Congress bills would need the Haiku lane (Oppose recall about 0.49). Use it to adjudicate the table, never to overwrite it, under the standing rule.

bearings.paper_claim: Firm size is associated with position type. At the 90th vs 10th employment percentile, larger firms are +19.5 pp more likely to lobby and +4.5 pp more likely to Monitor, with Oppose -1.8 pp and Amend -1.3 pp. These are associations, not causal effects.
bearings.system_side: Clients are classified by name (bank, credit union, other) with NAICS used only as linkage metadata. The system measured that its 22 pinned fintech and crypto firms hold 56 positions over 14 years, with one directional label. Directional positions sit with trade associations.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Kim's sample is Compustat firms with year fixed effects and makes no claim about associations. The system's observation (corporate filers mostly non-directional, associations directional) is consistent with it, but it is a descriptive count, not a replication. A coverage map of directional filers should weight associations, not firms.

gaps_exposed: There is no human-gold check of the Kim-format lane. All system benchmarks score agreement with Kim's labels, and 541 of the 876 benchmark pairs are Kim GNN predictions, which are about 78% accurate.
Kim positions end at the 117th Congress. Current-Congress coverage depends on the Haiku lane, whose Oppose and Support recall is about 0.49, so per-bill conflict for live bills is weakly measured.

Paul's 'reactive, not predictive' critique is unaddressed. Positions arrive after the quarterly deadline, so they cannot be features in the cosponsor forecaster without leakage controls. The forecaster currently uses no position features.
The positions wiring gap noted in the brain: an lda_rebuild ledger regeneration wipes the position columns, and lobby_position_join is not chained, so downstream priors can go stale silently.

No group-level latent scale (LPscore analogue) exists to place CU, bank, crypto and fintech associations on a shared axis. Such a scale would make 'conflicting industries' measurable, not only adjudicated.
flags: Possible conflict with D-021 and the standing rule that inferred positions are never automatic weights. efficiency_layers.py:175-211 puts signed_non_cu_opposition_z, built from inferred Oppose labels pushed onto members through the sponsor/cosponsor roster (org_stance_priors.py:631-700), into contest_index. That artifact is in run_pipeline and shown on the member desk. It moves no rank, but it is an LDA-derived weight inside a displayed score, and its member mapping is the refuted circular roster join. Paul should rule on whether it stays, is labelled UNVERIFIED, or is removed.

Paul's annotation calls the pipeline something to 'implement directly on an SNA vector graph'. Under D-021 (LDA is an identity source, not an edge or weight source) and the standing rule, Kim positions cannot become graph edges or weights. Flag this; do not recommend it.
Kim's best GNN configuration adds legislator-lobbyist prior-work (revolving-door) relations. If that relation is ever borrowed, influence language is barred on those edges.

The paper's 96.93% headline is measured on coder-agreed items only. Paul's position on melange-stance.debate-nli-classifier and melange-validation.gold-set-and-rank-gate cites it as LLM accuracy without that qualifier.

Internal inconsistencies to cite with care: the abstract says all bills, but the methods say enacted S./H.R. bills; the vetoed-stage pattern rests on 3 bills; SI Table 14/15 totals do not reconcile; the text says Support shows no difference, but SI Table 19 has Support significant at p<.10 in 2 of 5 specifications.

Every figure quoted from the system's benchmark (precision 0.42, recall 0.49, 0 of 23 Amend) is agreement with Kim labels on 876 overlap pairs from 2021-2022, not accuracy against human truth. Keep that window and denominator attached.
paul_alignment: Partly aligned, and partly stale. Paul's three findings (stage, firm size and Monitor, industry alignment) match the paper, though the stage result for failing bills is thin (3 vetoed bills). His call that the paper is a 'foundational pre-built pipeline' has already been acted on. The system downloaded the Dataverse release, rebuilt the labelling prompt on Haiku, and benchmarked it. That benchmark is why the pipeline is NOT used to feed the graph directly. Support and Oppose agreement is weak, and the standing rule plus D-021 keep LDA-derived positions as evidence, not edges or weights. His Weakness 2 (no inter-industry conflict per bill) is accurate about the paper's presentation, but the data allows it. The system already builds per-bill ALIGNED and OPPOSED labels for each sector pair, with a CCCA anchor (org_stance_priors.recompute_alliance_conflict), while the contested-bills registry stays display-only pending his ratifications. His Weakness 1 (reactive, not predictive) still holds and is not addressed. His margin note on conflicting industries is borne out by the industry boards' per-axis divergence. His notes do not record that the pipeline was benchmarked, nor that an inferred-Oppose count now feeds the displayed contest_index.

related.why: Same LDA/LobbyView source keyed by lob_id. The positions dataset joins directly onto LobbyView client and bill tables, which the system ingests.
Cited as ref 14. Its lobbying-network structure motivates the GNN graph of groups, bills and legislators in this paper.
The paper compares LPscores against DIME CFscores and finds r = 0.191 (n = 218): ideology from donations and positions from lobbying measure different behaviour.

Same LobbyView research group. It covers how the lobbying network changes over time, while this paper covers what position each group takes. Its legislator network runs to 2023, past this dataset's 2022 end.
The contested-bills registry's counterparty term cites Romero Moreno. Kim's per-bill Support/Oppose labels could supply the counterparty industries it needs.
Both tie firm size to lobbying behaviour. Huneeus and Kim estimate returns, while Kim et al. find larger firms lobby more and Monitor rather than Oppose.
Both use zero-shot LLM labelling of political text, with validation against human coders.
Both mine LDA congressional lobbying records. Harrison is the introductory pipeline guide; Kim adds position labels at scale.

Kim et al.'s per-bill Support/Oppose/Engage positions from LDA reports would be the way to observe Pritoni's issue-specific group alignments, such as who stands with CUs on a given bill. D-021 still limits LDA to identity, not edges.
This paper has bill positions for only about 17% of lobbied bills. Kim 2025's LLM-derived positions on the same LobbyView data would let a donation-lobbying link be signed by support or opposition.

extraction.theory: Access-purchase account: PAC contributions open doors that lobbyists then use, so PAC givers should also lobby and heavy lobbyists should have PACs. Election-targeting account: contributions mainly aim at electoral outcomes, so the two activities need not be linked; organizations can also lobby without donating. The authors treat the two as conceptually distinct: lobbying involves no direct transfer to members, while contributions do. They explicitly do not theorize why organizations choose one, both, or neither.
extraction.data: Center for Responsive Politics (CRP) data, curated from LDA Registrations and Activity Reports (LaPira and Thomas 2020) and FEC contribution disclosures by organizations and their officially affiliated PACs, linked by an expert-curated CRP crosswalk. Unit: organization (interest group). Period: 1998-2018 (even-numbered cycles in the figures). Sample sizes stated in the text: 9,076 organizations reporting political involvement in 1998; 15,729 in the 2008 cycle (text: "a decade later"). Figure 4 pooled counts over 1998-2018: Only Lobbies n=34,038; Only Contributes n=9,528; Lobbies and Contributes n=3,427; Not Active n=7,524 (sum 54,517, computed by the extractor). Lobbying totals include in-house and contract-firm lobbyists. Figure 1 cycle-level bar labels did not parse cleanly from the text layer, so only the figures stated in the prose are used here.
extraction.method: Descriptive only. Figure 1: yearly share of organizations that are lobby-only, PAC-only, or both. Figure 2: share of yearly lobbying expenditures and of PAC contributions by group type. Figure 3: distributions of average yearly PAC contributions (3a) and average yearly lobbying spending (3b) by group type, shown as dot plots with violin density, mean, IQR and 2.5/97.5 percentiles. Figure 4: log-log scatter of total lobbying spending against total PAC contributions per organization, with marginal histograms, coloured by the four activity categories. No regression, hypothesis test, or model is reported.
extraction.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claim and uses no identification strategy; it is a descriptive accounting of overlap.
extraction.scope: Population: US federal interest-group organizations that register to lobby under the LDA or are PAC or political-committee filers in CRP data, 1998-2018. Institution: Congress (lobbying) and federal candidate elections (contributions). Excluded by design: independent expenditures and Super PACs (note 1, p. 604); dark-money contributions (unobserved by definition, p. 599); contributions by employees and contract lobbyists, which are not counted as organizational giving (p. 599).

key_findings.finding: Most politically active organizations engage in only one of the two activities; only a small minority do both. The abstract states the headline finding, and the results section gives the counts.
key_findings.numbers: 1998 (n=9,076 orgs): 24% PAC-only, 64% lobby-only, 12% both. Around 2008 (n=15,729 orgs): 20% PAC-only, 70% lobby-only, 10% both. Percentages in each year sum to 100, so the categories are treated as exclusive.

key_findings.finding: Pooled over 1998-2018, only a small share of organizations do both.
key_findings.numbers: Lobby-only ~34,000 (n=34,038); PAC-only ~9,500 (n=9,528); registered but not active ~7,500 (n=7,524); both n=3,427 = 6.3% of the 54,517 total (6.3% is stated in the text; the 54,517 denominator is the extractor's sum).

key_findings.finding: Lobbying money is concentrated among organizations that also make PAC contributions, but that share fell over time.
key_findings.numbers: About 75% of lobbying expenditures (1998-2018) came from organizations that also contributed through PACs. The share of PAC contributions coming from organizations that also lobby fell from more than 65% in 1998 to about 30% in 2018.

key_findings.finding: Organizations that both lobby and contribute spend far more on lobbying than lobby-only organizations.
PAC contributions are higher on average among dual-activity organizations, and the distribution is very wide.
key_findings.numbers: Contribute-only: mean $7,857 (IQR $2,000-$33,566). Both: mean $31,167 (IQR $8,227-$1,082,366). The largest average contributors exceed $100 million (examples named: Crossroads GPS, Restore Our Future, Priorities USA).

key_findings.finding: The top lobbying groups spend the most and almost always have affiliated PACs, so most lobbying money comes from a few big spenders that also have PACs.
key_findings.numbers: No separate numeric estimate beyond the Figure 2 and Figure 3 results above.

key_findings.finding: Lobbying spending starts high and concentrates between $10,000 and $1 million, while PAC spending is more uneven, with many contributors giving under $10,000.
key_findings.numbers: Few lobbying organizations report under $10,000. Many PAC givers are under $10,000.

key_findings.finding: The authors restate the overlap as a yearly figure and note that organizations doing both are likely better resourced and, on average, more conservative. The conservatism point is cited to Crosson, Furnas and Lorenz (2020), not tested here.
key_findings.numbers: Only a 10% to 15% overlap between lobbying-registered and contributing organizations in any given year.

summary_md:
Furnas, LaPira and Brock (PS, Oct 2025) put Center for Responsive Politics LDA lobbying records and FEC records of organization and affiliated-PAC giving side by side for each organization, 1998-2018. Most politically active organizations do only one of the two. In 1998 (n=9,076 organizations), 64% only lobbied, 24% only gave through a PAC and 12% did both. By 2008 (n=15,729) the split was 70/20/10. Pooled over 1998-2018, 3,427 of 54,517 organizations (6.3%) did both. That denominator is the extractor's sum of the Figure 4 counts.

Within that minority sits most of the lobbying money. About 75% of lobbying spending in 1998-2018 came from organizations that also gave through a PAC. Their mean yearly lobbying spend was $403k, against $64k for organizations that only lobbied. Going the other way, the share of PAC dollars that came from lobbying organizations fell from over 65% in 1998 to about 30% in 2018. Employee giving, Super PACs and dark money are excluded. The paper is purely descriptive: no model, no identification strategy, and nothing about access or votes.

For Paul's systems the paper matters in three ways:

- **FEC as a stand-in for lobbying.** Across the population, campaign money is a poor proxy for lobbying. That supports the twice-locked rule that FEC exposure is never presented as a lobbying predictor. It also argues against reading the 42-month figure as a lead time: in the code it is only how much fresher the FEC data is than the LDA data.
- **The flip model's competitor-money leg.** That leg counts only PAC money. It can see the large trade associations, which almost all have PACs. It cannot see organizations that lobby without a PAC.
- **Mentat's counts.** Mentat matches individual employee giving by employer string. The paper's definition of organizational giving excludes employees, so its overlap figures do not carry over to Mentat's totals without first aligning the two definitions.

meta.title: Moneyed Interests, Information, and Action in Congress: A Survey Experiment
meta.venue: Prepared for the 115th Annual Meeting of the American Political Science Association (APSA), 2019. Working paper; manuscript header reads "APSR Submission Template". No journal publication is shown in the text.

extraction.title: Moneyed Interests, Information, and Action in Congress: A Survey Experiment
extraction.venue: Prepared for the 115th Annual Meeting of the American Political Science Association (APSA), 2019. Working paper; manuscript header reads "APSR Submission Template". No journal publication is shown in the text.
extraction.document_type: Conference working paper / unpublished manuscript (37 pages including Appendices A to C and references)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in six chunks, covering every line of the extracted file (lines 0 to 1937, PDF pages 1 to 37): front matter, abstract, introduction, data, experiment design, results, discussion, references, Appendix A (CCS methods, sampling, fielding, non-response balance), Appendix B (pairwise t-tests and Table 1), and Appendix C (question wording). Figures 1 to 5 are coefficient plots; only their captions and the text describing them were available, so no point estimates or confidence intervals are in the extracted text. Annotation JSON read in full: 48 items, all of type Highlight, all authored by Paul Goff, all with empty note content (no sticky-note text). Paul's paul_markup text is given as paraphrase rather than verbatim covered text, because the copyright limit allows one short quote; verbatim covered text stays in _annots/ff3529365037.json. The highlight colours carry no meaning in the file and are not interpreted. Metadata hint checked: title, authors and 2019 APSA venue match the text; doi left empty because the header holds only a placeholder (doi:xx.xxxx/xxxxx).
extraction.research_question: Whether and how congressional staffers respond to a lobbying-style request depending on (a) the identity of the requester (constituent, donor to the Member's campaign, national consumer-group lobbyist, large national business lobbyist), (b) the action requested (propose a new bill, or stop a bill under consideration), and (c) the supporting information offered (supportive constituency polling, the requester's own analysis, or jobs evidence from a center-left or center-right think tank). Four outcomes: likelihood of taking a meeting, of using the information for the boss's recommendations, of siding with the requester in the recommendation, and of rating the requester as representative of the district or state.
extraction.theory: No formal theory section; the paper states motivations and candidate mechanisms. (1) Staff act as gatekeepers and recommenders, so their choices carry weight (p.4). (2) Staff can exert independent effects on bosses' behaviour (p.4). (3) Elites, including senior staff, misperceive constituent opinion in ways that favour concentrated economic interests; the authors ask whether access alone changes staff behaviour (p.2, p.4). (4) Selective attention to information sources, driven by partisanship, may explain why Republicans respond to the well-off and Democrats to the disadvantaged (p.4). (5) Under time constraints, ideological think tanks act as heuristics for credibility and belief confirmation, and may create epistemic closure (p.16, p.18). (6) Status-quo bias and multiple veto points may explain why stop-bill requests succeed more often (p.18). The paper also proposes that donor influence may run through think tanks that fund agendas (p.3, p.17).
extraction.data: 2017 Congressional Capacity Survey (CCS), an online Qualtrics survey with an embedded vignette experiment. Fielded August 9 to November 4, 2017 (p.5; Appendix A gives August to December for the survey stage). Sampling frame: LegiStorm census of 8,485 prospective respondents in Washington, DC legislative-branch offices (633 organisational units; personal, committee, leadership and other offices), excluding purely administrative units (p.5, Appendix A). Final N = 441 respondents, response rate 5.2 percent (441 of 8,485), margin of error 4.5 percent at 95 percent (Appendix A). Subsample margins of error: House 5.9 percent, Senate 7.7 percent. Policy-domain blocks: budget 125 of 412 valid (MOE 8.7), health 120 of 412 (MOE 8.9), national security 167 of 412 (MOE 7.5); 6.6 percent missing. Unit of analysis: staffer-vignette rating. Appendix C factor-level counts each total 549 (identity: constituent 131, donor 128, corporation 154, consumer 136; action: propose 279, stop 270; information: left think tank 152, right think tank 136, own analysis 123, polling 138). The text does not explain why 549 exceeds 441 respondents, so respondents presumably rated more than one vignette, but the text does not say so. Party counts for the experimental subsamples are not reported. Post-stratification weights: maximum 4.82, minimum 0.749 (p.7). Stage 1 (Feb to Jun 2017, qualitative, non-random): 52 senior staff interviews, 4 former Members and 7 former staff (Appendix A). Respondent profile: 244 offices (133 House personal, 27 House committee or leadership, 60 Senate personal, 24 Senate committee or leadership); typical respondent is a 25 to 29 year old white male mid-level legislative assistant in a majority-party office with about four years on the Hill (p.5 fn.4).
extraction.method: Fully randomised 4 x 2 x 4 factorial vignette (32 possible conditions) with four dependent variables, each a five-point Likert item transformed to numeric. Following Hainmueller, Hopkins and Yamamoto (2014), the authors estimate the Average Marginal Component Effect (AMCE) of each factor level by OLS, using post-stratification weights and HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (p.9). Subgroup models for all staff, Democratic staff and Republican staff. The preregistered design called for 32-condition pairwise t-tests; the sample was underpowered for that, so these are reported in Appendix B. Appendix B: 11,904 pairwise tests (992 pairs x 4 outcomes, plus partisan subsamples); 828 pairs nominally significant at alpha 0.10; 46 pairs survive Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction at 0.10 (Table 1). Significant pairwise differences appear only for the "recommend the boss side with petitioner" and "representative" outcomes, mostly in the partisan subsamples and mostly between opposite-valence information sources. Figures 2 to 5 plot AMCEs with baseline categories: constituent, supportive polling, propose bill. Weights: post-stratification on chamber, office type and party from the LegiStorm frame; a second weight (psweight_g) conditions on gender because of persistent gender imbalance (Appendix A).
extraction.identification: Randomisation of the three vignette factors (identity, action, information) identifies each factor's effect as an AMCE, averaged over the joint distribution of the other factors (p.9). The text gives no separate identification argument. Respondent party is a pre-treatment attribute, so the Democratic versus Republican contrasts are subgroup comparisons, not randomised contrasts; the text makes no explicit claim about this. Outcomes are self-reported likelihoods for hypothetical requests, so they measure stated intention, not observed staff behaviour (the authors flag social desirability; see limitations).
extraction.scope: Population: congressional staff in Washington, DC legislative-branch offices who contribute to legislative operations, 2017 (115th Congress). Institution: US House and Senate personal, committee, leadership and other offices. Era: 2017, a period the authors describe as one of rising polarisation and inequality (abstract). The sample is restricted to DC-based staff, and the authors exclude purely administrative offices (p.5 fn.1). The findings are about stated responses to a single hypothetical lobbying scenario (job-creation evidence; one policy domain at a time), not about actual lobbying outcomes.

key_findings.finding: Taking a meeting (lowest-stakes outcome): most identity effects are not statistically distinguishable from zero. Democratic staff are less likely to take meetings with donors. Staff are less likely than constituents to take meetings with donors or lobbyists overall, but the authors read this as evidence that donors are not granted meetings more readily than constituents, and they flag social desirability. No relationship with information source or requested action.
key_findings.numbers: Figure 2 gives AMCEs only as a plot; no point estimates in the extracted text. Dependent variable: five-point Likert, numerically transformed.

key_findings.finding: Using the information provided: staff report being much less likely to use information from donors, especially Democratic staff. The only statistically distinguishable Democratic-Republican gap is for evidence from a center-right think tank. Other identity, action and information effects are not distinguishable from zero.
key_findings.numbers: No point estimates in the text; Democratic-Republican difference reported only qualitatively.

key_findings.finding: Siding with the requester in the recommendation to the boss (highest commitment): across all staff there is minimal evidence that think-tank information raises the chance of siding with the requester, and staff may be less likely to side with partisan-aligned groups than with individuals offering their own analysis. Disaggregated by party, Democrats are substantially more likely to side with center-left think tanks and less likely with center-right ones; Republicans show the mirror pattern. Offering information from a non-aligned think tank yields roughly twice the penalty of the benefit from an aligned one.
key_findings.numbers: 'Roughly twice' is the only ratio given; no coefficient values in the text.

key_findings.finding: Requests to stop a bill: both Democratic and Republican staff are more likely to side with requesters who want to stop a bill than with those proposing one. The authors offer several explanations (visibility of proposing bills, skepticism about legislation, status-quo bias from veto points, selectivity given many requests) and do not separate them.
key_findings.location: Results p.14 and Discussion p.18; Figure 4
key_findings.numbers: Not given in the text.

key_findings.finding: Perceived representativeness: all staff rate donors, business lobbyists and consumer lobbyists as less representative of their district or state than constituents. Exceptions: no distinguishable effect among Republican staff for donors or business lobbyists, and among Democratic staff for consumer lobbyists. Both parties rate presenters of aligned think-tank evidence as more representative than presenters of constituency polling supporting the staffer's own position. Republicans rate center-left presenters as less representative; Democrats' ratings of center-right presenters do not differ from polling presenters.
key_findings.numbers: Figure 5 AMCEs are plotted only; no point estimates in the text.

key_findings.finding: Staff are more likely to side with donors than to meet with or use information from donors, relative to constituents. The authors say this 'merits further inquiry' and do not resolve whether donors qua donors have direct influence.
key_findings.numbers: Not given in the text.

key_findings.finding: Headline conclusion: to influence Congress, bring policy evidence from an aligned partisan think tank. The authors read this both as evidence that staff want solid analysis, and as a warning of epistemic closure among partisan staff.
key_findings.numbers: Not applicable.

key_findings.finding: Pre-registered pairwise tests (Appendix B): only the recommend-to-side and representativeness outcomes yield significant pairwise differences after FDR correction; differences cluster in partisan subsamples where at least one information source has ideological valence. Authors describe these tests as considerably underpowered.
key_findings.numbers: 11,904 pairwise tests; 828 pairs nominally significant at alpha 0.10; 46 pairs significant after FDR correction at alpha 0.10 (Table 1 lists them with adjusted p-values).

key_findings.finding: Donor-meeting result contrasts with Kalla and Broockman (2016b): the authors find donors are not granted meetings more than geographic constituents, consistent with Chin, Bond and Geva (2000) but contrary to Kalla and Broockman. They note the chief of staff is the most likely staffer to grant donor meetings, citing Kalla and Broockman.
key_findings.numbers: Not given in the text.

limitations: Low response rate: 5.2 percent (441 of 8,485); margin of error 4.5 percent (Appendix A, p.5).

Underpowered design: the authors state the sample is substantially under-powered for the preregistered 32-condition pairwise tests and move to AMCEs (pp.8-9); Appendix B tests are described as considerably under-powered (p.33).
Social desirability: staff may over-report willingness to meet constituents and under-report willingness to meet donors; the authors caution about interpreting the donor result (pp.9-10, p.16).
Stated, hypothetical intentions rather than observed behaviour (vignette design, pp.7-8); the authors call the outcomes 'likelihood' ratings.

Non-response bias and imbalance: Table A2 shows significant unweighted and weighted differences on several covariates (e.g., gender, number of offices, office type, some title categories); weights do not remove all of them, and gender imbalance persisted, motivating a second weight (Appendix A).
Sample-size inconsistency: p.5 says the survey was sent to 8,458 staff, while the same page and Appendix A give 8,485 prospective respondents.
Unexplained counts: Appendix C factor-level counts sum to 549 per factor, more than the 441 respondents; the text does not explain this (likely repeated vignettes, unstated).
Party-subgroup counts are not reported in the text, so cell sizes for the Democratic and Republican subsamples cannot be checked.
Position in office (e.g., chief of staff versus others) is not analysed; deferred to future research (p.10).
Ideology is signalled through think-tank cues with brand names omitted (p.16); the authors do not test whether effects depend on brand recognition.
Donor effects: the authors state the experiment does not reveal preferential access to donors qua donors (p.3, p.17).
Stop-bill explanations (visibility, skepticism, status-quo bias, selectivity) are offered but not tested (p.18).
Replication data: the Appendix A codebook link is a placeholder ('<DATAVERSE OR OTHER PERMANENT REPOSITORY TO BE MADE AVAILABLE>', p.24); replication data are not yet available in this version.

Citation issues in the reference list: Kalla and Broockman (2016a) and (2016b) are the same article listed twice; several citations are 'n.d.' or 'in press' (Furnas n.d.; Crosson et al. in press; Furnas et al. in press; Grossmann and Isaac n.d.), so those works cannot be checked from this text.
Figures 2-5 are plots only in the extracted text; no coefficients, standard errors or confidence intervals are available here.

summary_md:
Furnas, LaPira, Hertel-Fernandez, Drutman and Kosar ran a 4 x 2 x 4 factorial vignette inside the 2017 Congressional Capacity Survey. The sample is 441 DC staffers, a 5.2% response rate (441 of 8,485), with 549 ratings per factor. Each vignette varied who made the request (constituent, campaign donor, consumer-group lobbyist or business lobbyist), what they asked for (propose a bill or stop one) and what evidence they brought (supportive polling, their own analysis, or a center-left or center-right think tank). Effects are AMCEs estimated by weighted OLS with HC3 errors. Figures 2-5 are plots, so the text gives no coefficient values.

Findings. Requester identity barely changes whether staff will take a meeting, and donors get no more meetings than constituents, which runs against Kalla and Broockman. Staff say they are less likely to use information from donors. Pooled across all staff, think-tank evidence does little for whether staff side with the requester. Split by party, the effect appears: staff side with evidence from their own side's think tank, and evidence from the other side costs about twice what aligned evidence gains. Staff in both parties side more often with requests to stop a bill than to propose one. Everything is stated intention about a hypothetical request, and the design is underpowered. After FDR correction, 46 of 11,904 pairwise tests survive.

For Paul's systems, the paper bears mainly on the partisan source-alignment factor (cpf_pressure 1.7/0.5, whose code comment cites "Furnas/Bakker") and on the flip model's premise that money buys access. It does not calibrate either one. The paper's manipulation is the ideology of an outside requester's evidence as judged by staff, not a co-partisan legislator applying pressure. Its asymmetry also runs the other way from the system's. Two places in the system attribute claims to this paper that it does not make: "money is capped, info is the lever" and "district-relevant information".

bearings.paper_claim: Pooled over all staff, there is minimal evidence that think-tank evidence raises siding with the requester. Split by party, aligned think-tank evidence raises siding and non-aligned evidence lowers it, and the non-aligned penalty is roughly twice the aligned benefit (Fig. 4). The comparison is against supportive constituency polling, not a neutral baseline. Stated intentions; N=441 staff, 549 ratings per factor; party subgroup cell sizes not reported.
bearings.system_side: cpf_pressure multiplies co-partisan member-to-member pressure by 1.7 and out-partisan pressure by 0.5. The kernel docstring cites 'Furnas/Bakker source-alignment' as the basis. Relative to 1.0, the system's gain (+0.7) is larger than its penalty (-0.5).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper randomises the ideology of an outside requester's evidence and records DC staffers' stated likelihood of siding with it (2017, single hypothetical). The system applies the factor to legislator-to-legislator cosponsor edges, where the partisan relation is between two Members, not an evidence source. That supports the direction of a source-alignment term, but not its 3.4 ratio or the gain-over-penalty asymmetry. If anything, the paper points to a penalty larger than the gain. The pooled estimate is null over the party fault line, so any figure taken from the paper must be quoted by party stratum or labelled UNSTRATIFIED.

This is contrary to Kalla & Broockman 2016 and consistent with Chin, Bond & Geva 2000. Staff say they are much less likely to use information from donors. They are relatively more likely to side with donors than to meet them or use their information, which the authors leave unresolved. The authors also find no preferential access for donors qua donors.

The vignette varies requester identity, not dollar amounts, so it says nothing about the shape of the saturating money term or about HALFF. Social desirability may push stated donor meetings down, as the authors warn, and that limits how far the evidence carries.

Taking a meeting, though, is the lowest-commitment step: it barely varies with requester identity, and whether staff side with a requester depends on the evidence's ideological alignment, not on access.

gaps_exposed: No direction-of-request asymmetry. Staff in both parties side more with requests to stop a bill than to propose one (Fig. 4, p.18). The flip, cascade and contested-bills machinery treat converting a target to pro and to anti symmetrically: equal money and peer pull give pflip 0.5 (flip_model.py:9-10). A block-vs-advance mode is absent; fec/lobbying/contested_bills.py is shipped but not wired.

No staffer or information layer between outside requester and Member. The system's source-alignment factor lives on Member-to-Member edges. The paper's effect sits on the outside requester's evidence as received by staff, and nothing in the engine models what evidence a CU requester brings or how aligned it is.

No requester-identity term. The paper shows that a trade-association or business lobbyist is rated less representative than a constituent. The engine has no term distinguishing who delivers the CU ask (constituent, PAC, ACU lobbyist).
No party-stratified calibration of cpf_pressure. The paper's pooled estimate is near null and its effects appear only within party strata, but the 1.7/0.5 constants are uncalibrated and unstratified.

Contradicts the 'access' half of the flip_model.py:21 comment ('money buys access/effort > votes ... Kalla & Broockman'), which this paper disputes for donor meetings.
paul_alignment: Paul's highlights pick out the paper's most careful claims: donors as donors show no preferential access; staff side with evidence from their own side's think tanks; staff side more with requests to stop a bill; and taking a meeting means much less than siding with a petitioner. The built system departs from those highlights in three places. First, the brain and dashboard comments recast the paper as 'money is capped, info is the lever' and 'co-partisan district-relevant information', claims Paul did not highlight and the paper does not make. Second, Paul's flip-model position ('money buys access and returns') is undercut on access by the very passage he highlighted. Third, the stop-bill asymmetry he highlighted twice (pp.14 and 18) has no counterpart in the engine. His annotation entries in the input point to Furnas et al. 2022 (PRQ) and Furnas, Heaney et al. 2019, not to this paper, and record no takeaways. The 2019 working paper therefore has no written takeaway in his notes, only the 48 highlights. The highlights are current and the system-side citations are stale.

related.why: Kalla & Broockman's field experiment finds donors get more access to senior staff. This paper's survey experiment finds donors get no meeting advantage over constituents, though both note the chief of staff is the most likely to grant donor meetings.

The system pairs the two papers as 'Furnas/Bakker source-alignment' for cpf_pressure and the lt-priming cross-party cue gate. Bakker covers partisan cue receptivity; Furnas covers staff reception of evidence from aligned and non-aligned sources.
Same lead author. It covers the partisan ties of lobbying firms, the supply side of the partisan-alignment effect this paper finds among staff.
Same author. It shows low overlap between lobbying and PAC spending, which is consistent with this paper's separation of donor identity from information-based lobbying.
Both study interest-group signals as cues inside Congress: Dear Colleague endorsements there, think-tank evidence here.

extraction.research_question: How can latent memberships of political actors in the communities that drive their observable interactions be inferred, when the network is bipartite, actors hold several memberships, and a pair of actors can interact in several ways? Application: which legislation communities organize interest-group lobbying of legislators in the 113th Congress, and when do domain-specific groups lobby outside their domain?
extraction.theory: Interest-group influence runs through repeated, narrow issue ties. Lobbying is organised into legislation communities that group interest groups with the legislators who hold relevant jurisdiction (e.g. Energy, Veterans' Affairs). Actors can have mixed memberships, because groups with broad interests and politicians with broad roles span several communities. A pair can also have mixed interactions, since one dyad's bills can belong to different issue communities. Industry-specific interests are the primary driver of lobbying; other motives play at most a secondary role. Social issues (the 'Civil Society' community) are the one broad cross-industry domain (pp. 10-11, 17). Power committees (Ways and Means, Appropriations) carry high-entropy politicians (p. 10). Anomalous dyads with more interactions than predicted suggest geography, campaign-contribution ties, or bill-specific stakes (p. 11). The model is motivated by the biSBM and mmSBM literatures (pp. 3-5).
extraction.data: Lobbying reports: 1,111,859 reports filed 1999-2017, yielding 2,396,693 issue corpora, 20,092 special interest groups and 1,164 current or former members of Congress (p. 7). Bills: 108,086 bills introduced in the 106th-114th Congresses were identified by NLP on lobbying reports (p. 2). About 12,000 bills are introduced per Congress, and most are lobbied by at least one group (Figure 2, p. 7). Analysis sample: the 113th Congress network. Unit: interest group i by politician j dyad, with A_ij = number of bills group i lobbied that politician j sponsored (p. 7). The main text does not state the 113th-Congress N of groups and politicians. Lobbied-bill distribution in the 113th Congress: median 3 groups per bill, maximum 946 (H.R. 1), and 23% of lobbied bills have one lobbying group (Figure 2 caption, p. 7). Session identification for bill references used report text signals, bill-text similarity, and 'Act of [YEAR]' phrases (p. 7).
extraction.method: Bipartite Link Community Model (biLCM): A_ij ~ Poisson(sum over z of kappa_z * alpha_iz * beta_jz), with z = 1..k link communities (eq. 1, p. 5). Estimation by EM with ancillary parameters q_ij(z) (eqs. 2-5, p. 6). Normalisation: sum_i alpha_iz = sum_j beta_jz = 1 for each z. k = 8 communities, chosen with reference to community structure seen in the latent space model (fn. 11). 50 random starts; highest likelihood kept (p. 6). Membership shares p_iz and q_jz are normalised kappa_z-weighted alphas and betas; entropy H in bits, with about 2^H communities actively used (p. 9). Comparison models: (a) 2-D latent space model with Poisson mean exp(alpha_i + beta_j - ||theta_i - psi_j||^2), Bayesian in Stan with hierarchical priors (eq. 6, pp. 12-13); (b) degree-corrected bipartite SBM (dc-biSBM), EM from Larremore et al. (2014), k = l = 8, 50 starts (eq. 7, pp. 15-16). Significance: permutation test against a null that keeps actor-level activity distributions (p. 12). Anomalies: observed versus biLCM-estimated counts, ranked by deviation (Table 1, p. 11).
extraction.identification: Not causal. The model is identified by the normalisation constraints on alpha and beta. Communities are latent structure inferred from co-lobbying counts; the paper makes no treatment-effect identification claim. Community names and committee matches are the authors' judgement from the leading groups in each community (p. 7).
extraction.scope: Population: interest groups and members of Congress who co-appear through lobbying disclosures (1999-2017 database), with the empirical application restricted to the 113th Congress (2013-2014). Institution: US Congress and federal lobbying disclosure. Era: 1999-2017 data; 113th Congress for estimates. The method is general to bipartite networks with mixed memberships; Section 3.4 (pp. 17-18) lists proposed uses in patronage networks, voter-politician contributions, roll-call ideal points and global value chains, none tested in the paper.

key_findings.finding: Eight legislation communities are named by their leading groups: Healthcare, Veterans' Affairs, Technology & Telecommunications, Energy, Finance & Insurance, Universities & Research, Civil Society, and Retail & Transportation.
key_findings.location: p. 7, paragraph 'We name the legislation communities'

key_findings.finding: Specialist groups lobby a single community; generalists spread across several. MICROSOFT and ARCH COAL interact with one community at probability of at least 85%. MCAFEE interacts with Technology & Telecom at 31% and Universities & Research at 52%. PHILIPS NORTH AMERICA and the CHAMBER OF COMMERCE have no single community above 25%.
key_findings.numbers: MICROSOFT, ARCH COAL: at least 85% in one community; MCAFEE: 31% and 52%; PHILIPS and CHAMBER: at most 25% per community

key_findings.finding: Specialist and generalist interest groups coexist. Targeted groups lobby committees with narrow jurisdiction; broad groups target power committees (Ways and Means, Senate Appropriations).
key_findings.numbers: not stated as a single statistic

key_findings.finding: Only one broad issue area is lobbied by diverse groups: Civil Society, covering social and human-rights legislation. It is the fourth most active of eight communities by kappa_z, so it accounts for only a modest share of lobbying activity.
key_findings.numbers: fourth of 8 by kappa_z

key_findings.finding: Politicians with high entropy, meaning membership in at least four communities, sit on power committees such as Ways and Means and Senate Appropriations, which control the power of the purse.
key_findings.numbers: entropy at least 2 corresponds to at least 4 communities; 52% of the 113th Congress were Republican (Figure 4 caption)

key_findings.finding: Politicians interacting with a community at probability at least 40% sit on committees matching its subject (e.g. Financial Services for Finance & Insurance; Armed Services for the defence-related group).
key_findings.numbers: threshold of 40% for committee groups

key_findings.finding: Anomalous dyads (observed far above biLCM prediction) are explained by geography, campaign contributions, or bill-specific stakes rather than shared issues. Examples: Tom Marino-CVS 10 observed vs 0.55 expected; Michael Enzi-eBay 11 vs 1.08; Jeanne Shaheen-Novo Nordisk 12 vs 1.61; Mike Conaway-iHeartMedia 7 vs 0.17.
key_findings.numbers: 10 dyads listed; largest gap Shaheen-Novo Nordisk 12 observed vs 1.61 estimated

key_findings.finding: Community structure is significant. In the permutation null (networks with the same actor-activity distributions), interest groups have much higher numbers of community memberships than in the observed network, so the observed network has strong community structure.
key_findings.numbers: not quantified in the main text (test details in Appendix B.2, not read)

key_findings.finding: The 2-D latent space model finds the same single-community clusters (e.g. Technology adjacent to Telecom and Energy; Universities adjacent to Industrial Research and Healthcare). Actors with mixed memberships fall in the centre of the latent space, where the LSM is uninformative. The paper attributes this to stochastic-equivalence confounding (Minhas et al. 2019).
key_findings.numbers: 2-D LSM; high-entropy hexagons cluster near the centre

key_findings.finding: The dc-biSBM recovers community boundaries that match the LSM clusters, and it finds two central communities (Civil Society and Retail & Transportation). It still assigns each actor to one community, so it misses mixed memberships. Chamber of Commerce, BP and McAfee fall in overlaps of community pairs.
key_findings.numbers: k = l = 8 for dc-biSBM

key_findings.finding: The biLCM is proposed as a general tool: for ideal-point estimation from roll calls treated as bipartite networks, for patronage and campaign-contribution networks, and for allocation of intermediate products in global value chains. These are proposed uses, not tested in the paper.
key_findings.numbers: none

limitations: The number of communities k must be chosen in advance; the paper calls for model selection or a Dirichlet-process prior (p. 17).
No covariates are used, though rich politician and group data exist (p. 17).
The model handles two-mode networks only; multi-partite interactions (group, politician, bill) are left to future work, e.g. tensor regression (pp. 17-18).
The data do not distinguish lobbying for from lobbying against a bill (p. 10), so alignment is inferred from co-lobbying only.
Lobbying reports do not name the politicians contacted; the network is built indirectly from sponsored bills (pp. 6-7).
Bill identification by NLP is error-prone, and session identification for bills referenced only by number is hard; the paper cites OpenSecrets misattributions (fn. 8, p. 7).
EM is not guaranteed to reach the global maximum, so the paper uses 50 random starts (pp. 6, 16).
The empirical application uses one Congress (113th); cross-session comparison is preliminary (fn. 5; Appendix B.3).
Anomaly explanations (geography, contributions, bill salience) are offered as suggestive and are not tested (p. 11).

summary_md:
Kim and Kunisky propose the Bipartite Link Community Model (biLCM). It is a Poisson model of a two-mode count matrix in which each interaction between an interest group and a politician is assigned to one of k latent "link communities". This allows mixed memberships, where an actor belongs to several communities, and mixed interactions, where one pair interacts in several communities. The model is fitted by EM with 50 random starts and k = 8. The application covers the 113th Congress only. A_ij counts the bills that group i lobbied and politician j sponsored, so the network is built indirectly because LD-2 reports never name the members contacted. The paper finds eight legislation communities that match committee jurisdictions. Specialists (MICROSOFT and ARCH COAL, at least 85% in one community) coexist with generalists (the CHAMBER OF COMMERCE, no community above 25%). Generalists and senior leaders cluster on power committees. Civil Society is the only cross-industry domain. The paper concludes that narrow industry interest drives most lobbying. A latent space model and a dc-biSBM recover the same blocks but miss mixed membership.

For Paul's systems, the most direct point is this. The paper's lobbying network uses the same construction as Melange's lobbied-member link: an organisation is credited to a member through a bill roster. The paper never treats that link as contact or influence, which backs the system's ruling that the link is circular. Three other bearings qualify claims the system makes. First, the dashboard cites the paper for "exploitable community structure" in the cosponsor graph, but the paper's communities are group-by-member lobbying communities, and budgetRecruit has no community term. Second, co-lobbying cannot separate lobbying for a bill from lobbying against it, so the paper cannot identify rival-industry champions. Third, leaders' broad memberships show how widely they draw lobbying, not leverage on credit-union issues. Everything here is descriptive, comes from one Congress, and is not causal.
