bearings.paper_claim: Lobbying reports do not name the politicians contacted, so the network is built indirectly: A_ij = number of bills group i lobbied that politician j sponsored. The resulting communities are read as co-attention structure, never as contact or influence. Window: 113th Congress; denominator: lobbied bills with an identified sponsor.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 6-7 (data construction; 'organizations need not identify their political contacts'); p. 10 (no for/against distinction)
bearings.system_side: The system builds client x bioguide x year counts by crediting every sponsor AND cosponsor of each lobbied bill (63,991 member-years). The brain records this link as circular: P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction, so it is refuted as influence evidence.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over directly, since the construction is the same and the system's version is broader (it adds cosponsors). The paper avoids circularity only because it makes no claim that lobbying predicts sponsorship. Any reuse in Melange must likewise stay descriptive. Under D-021 the matrix is an identity source and cannot become an edge or weight source. The paper uses sponsors only, so its A_ij is not identical to the system's dyads.

bearings.paper_claim: Communities are latent memberships in the bipartite interest-group x politician lobbying network (k = 8, 113th Congress). The central finding is that hard partitions miss mixed memberships: senior members and party leaders typically span at least 4 communities (entropy at least 2), and the LSM and dc-biSBM misplace these mixed actors.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 8-10 (Figures 3-4, entropy); pp. 12-16 (LSM and dc-biSBM comparison)
bearings.system_side: The grounding comment and the brain note cite Kim-Kunisky for 'the cosponsor network has real community structure the pathfinder exploits'. budgetRecruit is a max-coverage greedy over member-member cosponsor edges with Noisy-OR coverage and degree pruning. It contains no community detection or community term.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper does not carry over as cited. Its communities belong to a different graph (organisation-member lobbying, not member-member cosponsorship), and the code does not use communities at all. The citation should be removed or re-scoped. If a community-local recruitment term is ever added, the paper argues for mixed membership over a hard Louvain-style partition, because hub members are exactly the ones a partition misassigns.

bearings.paper_claim: Politicians who interact with a community at probability at least 40% sit on committees with matching jurisdiction (e.g. Financial Services for Finance & Insurance). Broad, generalist groups target power committees (Ways and Means, Senate Appropriations) instead. Window: 113th Congress; lobbying-attention counts, not outcomes.
bearings.paper_location: p. 10 (Figure 4 and committee analysis); p. 2 intro
bearings.system_side: Committee% = (Membership + Leadership)/2 / max, with seat weights set by owner-judged CU-relevance tier (Highly 3.0, Moderately 1.8, Slightly 0.9). The pillar assumes jurisdictional seats carry structural CU power.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Supports the premise that lobbying attention is organised by jurisdiction, so CU-relevant seats are where finance lobbying lands. It does not show that seats produce CU outcomes. Evidence is from one Congress, federal, and a different era from the 119th. The power-committee finding suggests checking how tax-writing and appropriations seats (CU tax status) are tiered; their tiers were not verified here.

bearings.paper_claim: Finance & Insurance emerges as a single legislation community. Because lobbying data do not distinguish lobbying for from lobbying against a bill, co-lobbying places rival interests together.
bearings.paper_location: p. 7 (community naming); p. 10 ('data do not distinguish between lobbying for or against')
bearings.system_side: Separate CU, bank, crypto and fintech boards, with a crown law that bars a Tier-1 champion from any sector's threat board. Industry rivalry is encoded through signed tensor valence and opposition priors.

bearings.system_side: Hand-set constants treat leadership as CU leverage: committee leadership Chair 1.0 to Member 0.2, and party leadership Speaker 1.0 to Minority Whip 0.2.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper shows that leaders attract lobbying across many domains, so any one industry's share of their attention is diluted. gaps_exposed: No mixed-membership or overlapping community model exists anywhere in the member SNA. Press HCoI uses Louvain hard partitions, which the paper shows misassign exactly the high-entropy hub members (leaders, power-committee members).

The org x member lobbying count matrix (lob_id, bioguide_id, year, n_bills) already exists but has no actor-activity-preserving null model. Any structure read from it is untested against a degree-preserving permutation baseline like the paper's.

The system has no residual or anomaly view: nothing flags organisation-member dyads that are unusually dense relative to issue alignment. These dyads are where the paper locates 'genuinely significant political connections' versus routine jurisdictional alignment.

No for/against signal attaches to LDA dyads (position ships empty, position_basis='not_disclosed'), so rival-industry structure cannot be read from lobbying co-attention. That needs a signed position source.
flags: CITATION MIS-TRANSFER: the dashboard's budget-mode grounding and the brain note in melange-dashboard-june-capstone cite Kim-Kunisky for exploitable community structure in the COSPONSOR network. The paper studies the bipartite lobbying network, and budgetRecruit (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:779-795) uses no community term. The citation overstates the grounding.

D-021: the paper's core object is an LDA-derived group x politician network. Any proposal to fit a biLCM and feed its memberships or dyad intensities into kernels, edges or weights would breach D-021. Diagnostic and descriptive use only.

Circularity: the paper's A_ij uses the same bill-roster join as the refuted lobbied-member link. Nothing in the paper licenses reading lobbied-to-sponsored co-occurrence as contact or influence, and the paper itself does not.

Not a rejected-SNA argument: the paper uses sponsors only and models actor activity through degree terms (kappa x alpha x beta, dc-biSBM). Neither is an argument to drop regular cosponsorship edges or to apply per-edge volume normalisation to the member graph, so neither rejected proposal should be read into it.

Window and denominator: every figure in the paper covers the 113th Congress (2013-14), with bills identified by NLP from 1999-2017 LDA reports. Do not quote its shares (85%, 25%, 40%) as properties of the 119th Congress or of CU lobbying.
paul_alignment: Partly aligned. Paul reads Kim and Kunisky as a tool for identifying champions (lobbied-member-link and industry-boards-crown). The paper does not support that reading. It measures shared co-lobbying attention, not alignment or contact, and its finance community would merge banks and CUs, so it cannot find rival-industry champions. His note is stale relative to the system: the system has since ruled the same bill-roster construction circular (P(joined | lobbied) = 1), which the notes do not reflect. His committee-pillar citation (money and lobbying concentrate in jurisdictional committees) is supported by the 40%-threshold committee-matching result. His leadership citation is supported as breadth, not leverage. His path-finding gap, turning bipartite lobbying data into a graph path-finding can run on, is real, but the dashboard's current Kim-Kunisky citation for budget mode claims more grounding than the code uses. No annotation was recorded in his takeaways for this work.

related.why: The biLCM network is distilled from the LobbyView bill-level lobbying database (Kim 2018). It shares that NLP bill-identification pipeline and its misattribution risks.
It supplies the signed bill positions (support, oppose, engage) that Kim-Kunisky lack. Without such positions, co-lobbying cannot separate rival industries.
Committee community structure in the House; Kim-Kunisky match their lobbying communities to the same committee jurisdictions. Both are cited together in the dashboard's grounding.
It extends lobbying-network analysis over time with issue codes, where Kim-Kunisky give a single-Congress snapshot and leave cross-session comparison preliminary.
It takes a multi-partite (hypergraph) approach to a lobby network, which addresses the group-politician-bill limitation Kim-Kunisky leave to tensor methods.
It uses signed partitioning of the legislator network. That supplies the sign that Kim-Kunisky's unsigned co-lobbying lacks, but it is still a hard partition without mixed membership.
